title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Grattan enacts 8-month data center halt while Ypsilanti targets power lines for U-M plans

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into why more townships are hitting the brakes on these massive projects.
Let's start with the lead story out of Kent County.
Grattan Township's board voted Monday for an eight-month moratorium on new data centers.
It expires April 30, 2027, and it came on a recommendation from their legal counsel.
Exactly. This fits a pattern we've seen building across the state this summer.
Why are these pauses happening now? What's the bigger pressure point?
Data centers need enormous amounts of power and water, and local officials are realizing the grid and aquifers weren't built for that scale.
So it's not just one township reacting to one proposal.
Right. Grattan is looking at the same issues Ypsilanti Township tackled today with its own moratorium on large utility structures tied to the University of Michigan's supercomputer expansion.
That one specifically blocks infrastructure that could feed heavy electricity users.
Yes, and it gives officials time to study impacts on power demand and land use before anything gets locked in.
How does this affect everyday residents who aren't right next door?
Washtenaw County residents could see delayed projects, but also potential ripple effects on regional utility rates if demand keeps spiking.
What about the noise and traffic stories we've been hearing?
The Detroit Free Press piece today shows people living beside existing centers dealing with constant equipment hum and higher bills already.
So the concerns aren't theoretical anymore.
No, and that's feeding into why Grattan and others are acting before more facilities come online.
Let's talk about the land angle too. There's that golf course sale near Saline.
Related Digital bought Rustic Glen to expand near the big Oracle campus. That adds years of construction pressure on roads, power lines, and water.
And Saline is pressing the state on wastewater permits for millions of gallons.
Township officials want EGLE to explain how it protects local wells, since downstream communities share the aquifer.
What happens next in these places after a moratorium passes?
Officials use the time to write rules on noise, water use, energy efficiency, and decommissioning.
We've seen that in Ypsilanti's planning commission agenda tonight.
Exactly. They're holding public hearings on zoning text amendments that would set standards for all those things.
How many other townships have done something similar recently?
It's becoming a common tool. Grattan's eight months gives them breathing room similar to what others have sought this year.
And there's that resident in one township who tried to recall officials over a data center vote and lost.
She's now pushing for broader changes in how these votes are handled statewide.
So accountability questions are rising too.
Yes, and that could shape how future projects get approved or blocked.
What about the Oakland County project that's heading to a make-or-break vote?
Lawsuits and state rules are creating uncertainty there, and the outcome could set precedent for metro Detroit suburbs.
Tax revenue versus power demand is the classic tradeoff.
Residents will feel changes in both if it advances.
Back to Grattan for a minute. Who are the main players pushing for or against these pauses?
Local boards and residents concerned about farmland conversion and infrastructure strain versus developers and sometimes utilities wanting to move fast.
Any sense of how long these fights usually last?
They've been stretching out over months as more proposals surface near existing campuses like Oracle's in Saline.
What could break the logjam at the state level?
Clearer rules from EGLE on wastewater and from the utilities on how new demand gets allocated without raising everyone's bills.
That seems to be what the Ypsilanti and Grattan pauses are buying time for.
Precisely. Local control while the bigger picture gets sorted.
Okay, let's move to quick hits. Starting with the Detroit-area resident stories.
The Free Press reports concrete effects: constant hum, traffic, and higher utility bills for neighbors.
And that one voter pushing rule changes after her recall bid failed.
She wants broader reforms so townships handle these votes differently going forward.
On the Saline side, the golf course purchase adds to the Oracle expansion pressure.
Related Digital now controls more land right next to the $43 billion campus.
Ypsilanti Township also enacted a full land-use moratorium blocking new data center proposals.
That one studies roads, power, and noise impacts before anything moves ahead.
And separately they halted big utility builds tied to the U-M supercomputer.
Both moves aim to give locals more say before industrial-scale development locks in.
Oakland County's project is still at that pivotal local decision point.
Lawsuits and state rules keep the uncertainty high there.
Now for on deck.
Tonight the Ypsilanti Planning Commission holds a public hearing on zoning ordinance text amendments for data centers.
That covers definitions, noise standards, water use, energy efficiency, and decommissioning rules.
The City of Ypsilanti Planning Commission has the same hearing on its agenda.
Listeners can attend either one if they're in the area.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Grattan Township Pauses Data Centers as Ypsilanti Freezes Utility Builds
